title: You asked, we answered: Why are central banks moving their gold reserves
gist: De Nederlandsche Bank's September 2026 transfer of ~86t of gold from New York and Ottawa to London — which made London (32.1%) the largest single storage location for Dutch gold, above domestic holdings (30.8%) — marks a shift in official-sector thinking from repatriation toward optimising custody risk, physical accessibility and market liquidity. The World Gold Council argues this is active reserve-location management, not a prelude to selling, with its 2026 survey showing a record 45% of central banks expecting their gold holdings to rise and only 1% expecting a decline.

insights.claim: On 2 September 2026 De Nederlandsche Bank announced it had transferred approximately 86 tonnes of gold from New York and Ottawa to London in an operation conducted between March and August 2026, explicitly to improve the liquidity and tradability of its reserves and strengthen preparedness for severe crises.
insights.speaker: @goldcouncil
insights.so_what: Establishes that a G10 central bank is now optimising for tradability rather than proximity — watch London vault balances and LBMA clearing volumes for further official-sector inflows.
insights.quote: The operation, conducted between March and August 2026, was designed to improve the liquidity and tradability of DNB’s gold reserves and strengthen its preparedness for severe crises.
insights.locator: Gold on the move

insights.claim: London's share of Dutch gold reserves rose from 18.1% to 32.1%, surpassing domestic holdings of 30.8% and making London rather than the Netherlands the largest single storage location for Dutch gold, while New York and Ottawa each fell to 18.5% from 31.3% and 19.7% respectively.
insights.speaker: @goldcouncil
insights.so_what: A concrete measure of de-risking away from North American custody that other reserve managers may benchmark against.
insights.locator: At first glance, the decision might look

insights.claim: Roughly 59t of the DNB operation was executed as a sale in New York with replacement by internationally tradable gold in London, while just over 27t was physically flown from North America to DNB's Zeist facility and a similar quantity moved from Zeist to London — meaning the headline 86t figure overstates the physical transatlantic shipment.
insights.speaker: @goldcouncil
insights.so_what: Location-switch trades are executed via sale-and-replacement in the OTC market, so headline repatriation numbers are a poor proxy for physical bullion flows or freight demand.
insights.quote: This was therefore a strategic reallocation of reserve locations, not simply 86t of bullion being flown across the Atlantic.
insights.locator: The mechanics were equally significant

insights.claim: DNB reversed its own 2014 direction of travel: having moved gold from New York to Amsterdam to raise the domestic share, in 2026 it moved gold from North America predominantly to London to make it more readily deployable, with the author framing both as the same objective of resilience through purposeful distribution.
insights.speaker: @goldcouncil
insights.so_what: Signals that 'bring it home' is no longer the default reserve-management reflex — deployability now competes with sovereignty as the binding constraint.
insights.quote: These decisions point in different geographical directions, but share the same objective: resilience through a more purposeful distribution of reserves.
insights.locator: DNB's decision captures this evolution

insights.claim: Gold repatriation predates the post-crisis geopolitical era: Germany transferred around 930t from London to Frankfurt in 2000, with the Bundesbank later confirming the gold had been inspected and that some bars were to be recast to meet Good Delivery standard.
insights.speaker: @goldcouncil
insights.so_what: Reframes repatriation as a long-running reserve-management practice rather than a novel geopolitical signal, tempering alarmist readings of each new transfer.
insights.locator: From repatriation to location strategy

insights.claim: The 2011-2019 wave of relocations was driven by national control and public confidence, with Venezuela returning 160t in 2011-12, Germany moving 674t from New York and Paris to Frankfurt between 2013 and 2017, the Netherlands moving 122.5t from New York to Amsterdam in 2014, and Austria moving 90t out of London between 2015 and 2018.
insights.speaker: @goldcouncil
insights.so_what: Quantifies the historical baseline against which the current wave should be judged — hundreds of tonnes have already shifted custody without disrupting the gold market.
insights.locator: Venezuela returned 160t from foreign institutions

insights.claim: Even in the control-driven second wave, most central banks pursued balanced rather than fully domestic strategies — Germany targeted half its reserves in Frankfurt, Austria ended with half domestic while retaining substantial London and Switzerland holdings to preserve market access, and Poland paired repatriation with a major expansion of its gold reserves.
insights.speaker: @goldcouncil
insights.so_what: Full repatriation is the exception, not the trend — overseas trading-centre vaulting keeps a structural floor under London and Swiss demand.
insights.locator: In the second wave, from roughly 2011 to 2019

insights.claim: The cohort of countries reviewing gold storage has broadened materially since 2020, with Serbia reportedly returning around 13t in 2021-22, India progressively increasing domestic gold holdings since 2022 with the pace of relocation accelerating sharply after March 2023, and Türkiye changing the overseas custody location of part of its gold.
insights.speaker: @goldcouncil
insights.so_what: Custody review is spreading from a handful of European cases to emerging-market reserve managers, widening the addressable market for vaulting and logistics providers.
insights.locator: The range of countries reviewing or changing

insights.claim: France changed the geographical distribution of its gold exposure in 2025-26 by selling 129t held in New York and acquiring an equivalent quantity of replacement gold in Europe, an operation the Banque de France did not describe as a physical relocation.
insights.speaker: @goldcouncil
insights.so_what: A second major European central bank cutting New York custody exposure within a year — a synchronised pattern worth tracking in IMF/central bank reserve disclosures.
insights.locator: France also changed the geographical distribution

insights.claim: Reported changes in custody position do not reliably prove physical shipment of gold, since location changes can involve moving bullion between foreign custodians or selling in one market and buying replacement metal in another without altering the quantity owned.
insights.speaker: @goldcouncil
insights.so_what: A caution for anyone modelling physical flows off repatriation headlines — the accounting and the metal often move separately.
insights.quote: Changes in custody position do not always prove physical shipment.
insights.locator: Chart 1: Selected central bank repatriations

insights.claim: Central banks are increasingly optimising gold storage across three explicit considerations — custody risk, physical accessibility and market liquidity — rather than treating domestic storage as the single correct answer.
insights.speaker: @goldcouncil
insights.so_what: The most portable mental model in the piece: use it to predict which hubs win official-sector flows — those scoring well on all three, i.e. London, and increasingly Singapore and Hong Kong.
insights.quote: Central banks are increasingly optimising across three considerations: custody risk, physical accessibility and market liquidity.
insights.locator: The third wave is more complex

insights.claim: Heightened geopolitical uncertainty has raised official-sector attention on jurisdiction, access during a crisis and exposure to overseas financial infrastructure, but the recent French and Dutch operations show the answer does not necessarily lie in domestic storage alone.
insights.speaker: @goldcouncil
insights.so_what: Counters the popular narrative that geopolitical stress mechanically implies repatriation — the flow can go to a rival trading hub instead of home.
insights.locator: The third wave is more complex

insights.claim: Security alone is no longer a sufficient standard for official gold reserves; for some central banks the metal must also be accessible, tradable and distributed across locations that remain dependable under stress.
insights.speaker: @goldcouncil
insights.so_what: Implies persistent demand for Good Delivery-eligible, market-deliverable bars in major hubs rather than static domestic vaulting.
insights.quote: But the emerging picture is one in which security alone is no longer enough.
insights.locator: Recent transfers should therefore not be interpreted

insights.claim: The World Gold Council's 2026 Central Bank Gold Reserves Survey found the Bank of England remains the most commonly cited vaulting location, used by 57% of respondents, while 49% reported holding at least some gold domestically.
insights.speaker: @goldcouncil
insights.so_what: London's custody franchise is still dominant despite years of repatriation headlines — a structural advantage for LBMA-linked liquidity.
insights.locator: What central banks themselves are saying

insights.claim: Over the preceding 12 months 9% of surveyed central banks had increased domestic storage while a larger 10% had diversified their overseas storage locations, undercutting the assumption that the dominant trend is onshoring.
insights.speaker: @goldcouncil
insights.so_what: Overseas diversification is now running at least level with repatriation — position for multi-hub vaulting demand rather than a one-way flow home.
insights.locator: Over the preceding 12 months

insights.claim: Looking forward, 7% of surveyed central banks planned to increase domestic storage while 9% expected to diversify further overseas — with the overseas-diversification figure having jumped from just 2% in the previous survey.
insights.speaker: @goldcouncil
insights.so_what: A 2%-to-9% jump in stated intent to diversify overseas is the sharpest directional signal in the survey — a leading indicator for new vaulting hub mandates over the next year.
insights.quote: The latter figure rose from just 2% in the previous survey.
insights.locator: Looking ahead, 7% planned to increase

insights.claim: The survey base of 69 gold-holding central banks splits 16 advanced economies to 53 emerging market and developing economies, so aggregate custody-intent readings are heavily weighted toward EMDE reserve managers.
insights.speaker: @goldcouncil
insights.so_what: Read headline survey percentages as primarily an EMDE signal, not a developed-market one, when extrapolating to reserve flows.
insights.locator: Chart 2: Where do you currently vault your gold reserves?

themes.theme: Relocation is not a sell signal

insights.claim: Moving gold into a more liquid market should not be read as preparation for a sale, because liquidity is valuable precisely as optionality in an extreme event and building that capability says nothing about whether a central bank expects to use it.
insights.speaker: @goldcouncil
insights.so_what: Pushes back against a bearish interpretation of official-sector transfers to London — don't front-run supply that may never come.
insights.quote: But liquidity is valuable precisely because it provides options in an extreme event.
insights.locator: Movement does not mean an intention to sell

insights.claim: DNB was explicit that it did not expect to deploy the transferred gold, framing the objective as ensuring reserves would be more readily available if required.
insights.speaker: @goldcouncil
insights.so_what: Direct issuer guidance that the 86t move is contingency preparation, not latent supply overhang.
insights.locator: DNB was explicit that it did not expect

insights.claim: The 2026 survey found only 1% of respondents expected their own gold reserves to decline over the next 12 months while a record 45% expected them to increase.
insights.speaker: @goldcouncil
insights.so_what: A record intent-to-buy reading with near-zero intent to sell supports a continuing official-sector demand bid under the gold price.
insights.quote: only 1% of respondents expected their own gold reserves to decline over the next 12 months, while a record 45% expected them to increase
insights.locator: At the same time, the 2026 survey found

insights.claim: Future official-sector custody adjustments may involve a wider range of hubs, with Singapore having announced planned vaulting services for foreign central banks and sovereign entities and Hong Kong expanding its gold clearing, settlement and storage infrastructure.
insights.speaker: @goldcouncil
insights.so_what: Asian hubs are building to compete with London and New York for official-sector gold custody — a multi-year share-shift theme in vaulting, clearing and settlement infrastructure.
insights.quote: Singapore has announced planned vaulting services for foreign central banks and sovereign entities, while Hong Kong is expanding its gold clearing, settlement and storage infrastructure.
insights.locator: Future adjustments may also involve a wider range of hubs
